title: Bridges and Structures
summary: Types of bridges (beam, truss, arch, cantilever, suspension and cable-stayed), how each carries loads, forces in bridge members, and choosing a bridge design.

notes.text: A **bridge** is a structure that **spans** (crosses) an obstacle such as a river, valley or road. The **span** is the distance between supports. Bridges must carry their own weight (**dead load**, static) and moving traffic and wind (**live load**, dynamic).

rows: A horizontal beam rests on supports (piers or abutments) at each end. The top of the beam is in compression and the bottom in tension.
Short spans; simple and cheap (footbridges, highway overpasses)
A beam strengthened with a triangulated frame (truss) of struts and ties
Medium spans; strong and light (railway bridges)
The curved arch carries the load outwards and down to strong abutments; the arch is in compression
Medium spans; often built of stone or concrete (Bloukrans Bridge in the Garden Route is a concrete arch)
Each half is a cantilever (a beam supported at one end only) projecting from a pier; the two arms meet in the middle
Medium to long spans where supports cannot be placed in the middle
The deck hangs from vertical cables attached to two main cables, which pass over tall towers and are anchored at each end; cables in tension, towers in compression
Cables run directly from tall towers (pylons) to the deck in a fan or harp shape
Long spans; modern (Nelson Mandela Bridge in Johannesburg)

notes.label: Remember
notes.text: A **cantilever** is a beam fixed at one end only, like a diving board or a balcony. The top is in tension and the bottom in compression.

notes.title: Choosing a bridge type
notes.problem: A wide, deep river with busy shipping needs a long crossing with no piers in the water. Which type is best: beam, arch or suspension?
steps: A beam bridge needs piers at short intervals, which would block ships.
An arch has limited span and needs firm banks.
A suspension bridge spans very long distances, with towers only near the banks.

items: **Compression**: pillars, arches, towers and the top of beams.
**Tension**: cables, ties and the bottom of beams.
**Torsion**: twisting caused by strong winds (the Tacoma Narrows Bridge in the USA collapsed in 1940 because wind made it twist and sway).

items: **Ground conditions**: can supports be built in the river? Are the banks strong enough for arch abutments?
**Materials and cost**: steel, reinforced concrete, timber, rope.
**Environment and appearance**: impact on rivers and wildlife; looks.
**Ships**: does the bridge need to be high or open to let boats pass?

notes.title: Testing a model bridge
notes.problem: Learners build a paper beam bridge spanning 300 mm. It collapses with a load of 150 g. Suggest how to make it stronger without adding more paper.
steps: Fold or corrugate the paper to make the deck stiffer.
Roll paper into tubes for beams.
Add a triangulated truss along the sides.
Use an arch shape below the deck.
notes.answer: Change the shape: folding, tubes, triangulation or an arch.

questions.prompt: A car drives onto the middle of a beam bridge. Which part of the beam is in compression and which in tension?
questions.memo:
✓ The top of the beam is in compression (1)
✓ The bottom of the beam is in tension (1)

questions.prompt: Name the forces in the cables and the towers of a suspension bridge.
Give THREE factors an engineer must consider when choosing a bridge design.
questions.memo: Any three (1 each): span; type of load; ground conditions; materials; cost; environmental impact; appearance; need for ships to pass

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between dead load and live load on a bridge.
questions.memo:
✓ Dead load: the bridge's own weight; static (1)
✓ Live load: moving traffic, people and wind; dynamic (1)
